summary: We identified the Cerro Guacha region in the Bolivian Andes as a promising terrestrial analogue for testing perchlorate-removal technologies for future Mars bases. Perchlorates in Martian soil present a challenge to using local resources for water and agriculture, making suitable Earth testing sites important for developing effective treatment methods. To select this location, we developed a satellite-based screening framework using NASA MODIS temperature and vegetation observations, NASA GPM precipitation data, and Copernicus elevation data. Our analysis compared nighttime temperatures, rainfall, vegetation, elevation, and day–night temperature differences across candidate environments. Published perchlorate occurrence records and soil chemistry measurements from NASA’s Phoenix mission provided the chemical reference for our assessment. The analysis highlighted Cerro Guacha’s combination of cold, dry conditions, sparse vegetation, and high elevation, leading us to select it as a candidate for perchlorate-removal studies. Our results include maps and environmental comparisons supporting this choice. Cerro Guacha could serve as a testing ground for perchlorate-removal methods before they are used to treat soil and water on Mars.
details:
Our project presents the Cerro Guacha region in the Bolivian Andes, near 22.7°S, 67.5°W, as a candidate analogue for testing perchlorate-removal methods for future Mars bases. Perchlorates in Martian soil create challenges for water use and cultivation. We focused on identifying an Earth location where relevant environmental conditions could support the development and testing of treatment methods.

We selected the region through satellite analysis carried out in Google Earth Engine using JavaScript. Our team developed a screening framework that compared nighttime surface temperature, precipitation, vegetation, elevation, and day–night temperature differences across candidate environments. NASA MODIS provided surface-temperature observations and vegetation indices, NASA GPM supplied precipitation data, and Copernicus DEM provided elevation data. Additional MODIS albedo and land-cover layers helped identify bright, sparsely vegetated surfaces and filter unsuitable areas.

The code generated environmental similarity maps, candidate rankings, and tables exported as CSV files. We also plotted published perchlorate localities as reference points alongside the satellite results. These records provided regional geochemical context, while the environmental analysis highlighted Cerro Guacha’s combination of cold temperatures, low precipitation, sparse vegetation, and high elevation. Together, the maps and comparisons supported our choice of this part of the Bolivian Andes.

We designed the comparison around a specific task: perchlorate removal. This gave the site selection a practical purpose and brought together satellite observations, published geochemical records, and the requirements of future Mars resource use. Our team considered both the environmental similarities and the relevance of those conditions to treatment experiments. The resulting site assessment gives researchers a defined geographic target and the evidence behind its selection. Cerro Guacha could serve as a testing ground for perchlorate-removal methods before they are used to treat soil and water on Mars.
